## `M` is a group, and is generated by transvections

Any finite subset of `M` is supported on a finite index set `S`, where the
matrices form the ordinary finite upper unitriangular group; `A` is nilpotent
there, so `(I+A)^-1 = I - A + A^2 - ...` terminates.  Within such an `S`,
eliminating the first, second and later superdiagonals by elementary
transvections writes any element as a product of `x_(ij)(a)`.

## Torsion-freeness

Let `A != 0` have finite ordered support and let `i < j` realize its first
nonzero superdiagonal, meaning no shorter gap carries a nonzero entry.  Every
`A^k` with `k >= 2` vanishes at `(i,j)`, because a factorization through an
intermediate index would use two strictly shorter gaps.  Hence the `(i,j)`
entry of `(I+A)^n - I` is `n A_(ij) != 0` for `n > 0`.

## Perfectness

Given `i < j`, density of `Q` supplies `k` with `i < k < j`, and matrix
multiplication gives

```text
[x_(ik)(a), x_(kj)(1)] = x_(ij)(a).
```
Every generator is a commutator, so `M = [M,M]`.

## No finite-dimensional representations

For `i < k < j` the indices `{i,k,j}` carry a copy of `UT_3(Q)` inside `M`,
whose centre contains every `x_(ij)(a)`.  The first prerequisite proves that
every exact finite-dimensional unitary representation of `UT_3(Q)` kills its
centre: on a central-character block of dimension `m`, determinants applied
to `[x(a),y(b)] = z(ab)` give `chi(ab)^m = 1`, and then `a = c/m`, `b = 1`
give `chi(c) = 1`.  Restricting any `rho : M -> U(d)` to that copy therefore
kills `x_(ij)(a)`.  These generate `M`, so `rho` is trivial and
`Rad_fd(M) = M`.

## MF

Take increasing finite `S_n subset Q` exhausting the index set and increasing
primes `p_n`.  The subgroup of `M` supported on `S_n` with all entry
denominators prime to `p_n` reduces to the finite group
`UT_(|S_n|)(F_(p_n))`, and reduction respects products.  So every finitely
generated subgroup of `M` is residually finite: a fixed nonzero rational
entry stays nonzero modulo all sufficiently large primes, and the finitely
many denominators involved are eventually invertible.  `M` is the directed
union of these subgroups, so it is locally residually finite, hence LEF,
hence operator MF by the second prerequisite.

Explicitly, the left regular permutation representations of the finite
quotients give maps `V_n` with `V_n(1) = I`, exact multiplicativity on any
fixed pair for all large `n`, and `||V_n(m) - I|| >= sqrt 2` eventually for
`m != 1`, which is the operator-norm definition directly.

## Not finitely generated

A finite subset lies in the subgroup supported on a finite index set, which
is closed under products and inverses, while `M` contains transvections on
arbitrarily many indices.
